summary: Extends Mobile IP to support reverse tunnels, where traffic from a mobile node is sent back through its home agent. This keeps packets topologically correct when networks filter based on source addresses. It does not try to solve firewall problems. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A mobile device keeps the same address when it travels. When it sends packets from a new network, those packets carry an address that belongs to a different network, and routers that check source addresses throw them away. This document describes how to send the traffic back through the device's home agent so it survives that check.

what is reverse tunneling in mobile ip
what is the t bit in mobile ip
why does mobile ip need reverse tunnels
subtitle: How a roaming Mobile IP device sends its traffic back through its home agent so source addresses stay topologically correct.

tldr.problem: When a device moves to another network, its packets leave with a home address that does not belong to the network they are leaving from, and routers that filter on source addresses will drop them.
tldr.mechanism: The document adds a bit to the Mobile IP messages that asks for a reverse tunnel, and two ways to build it. The foreign agent either intercepts the device's plain packets or receives them already encapsulated, and in both cases sends them to the home agent inside another IP header.
tldr.outcome: The packets that reach the Internet carry the foreign agent's care-of address on the outside, so filtering routers accept them. The document obsoleted RFC 2344 in 2001.

today: RFC 3024 is a Proposed Standard on the IETF Standards Track. It replaced RFC 2344 in 2001, adding support for disparate address spaces and making the encapsulating delivery style optional, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It extends the Mobile IP specification in RFC 2002.

sections.title: Why Reverse Tunnels Are Needed
sections.content:
Mobile IP assumes that IP unicast datagrams are routed on the destination address and not on the source address. Because of security concerns such as IP spoofing attacks, and in line with the advice in RFC 2267 and the CERT advisories, routers that break this assumption are increasingly common. In the presence of such routers, the source and destination addresses in a packet must be topologically correct.

The forward tunnel complies with this, because its endpoints, the home agent address and the care-of address, are properly assigned addresses for their respective locations. The source address of a packet transmitted by the mobile node does not correspond to the network prefix from where it emanates. A forward tunnel shuttles packets towards the mobile node and runs from the home agent to the mobile node's care-of address. A reverse tunnel runs the other way, from the care-of address to the home agent.

Reverse tunnels have uses whatever their topological correctness: they let mobile routers avoid recursive tunneling, they let a mobile node join multicast groups in its home network and send multicast packets that appear to come from there, and they save the time-to-live of packets sent to the home network, since a tunnel counts as one decrement.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers usually deliver a packet by looking at where it is going, not where it came from. Some routers also check that the source address belongs to the network the packet came from. A roaming device fails that check, so its traffic has to be wrapped in another header that does pass.

sections.title: How the Pieces Fit Together
sections.content:
A mobile node arrives at a foreign network, listens for agent advertisements and selects a foreign agent that supports reverse tunnels. It requests that service when it registers through the chosen foreign agent, and at the same time asks for either the Direct or the Encapsulating delivery style.

In the Direct Delivery Style, the mobile node designates the foreign agent as its default router and sends its packets to it directly, without encapsulation. The foreign agent intercepts them and tunnels them to the home agent. In the Encapsulating Delivery Style, the mobile node encapsulates all its outgoing packets to the foreign agent, which decapsulates them and re-tunnels them to the home agent using its own care-of address as the entry point of the new tunnel.

The document assumes a common IP address space between the mobile node and the home agent, and that the reverse tunnels are symmetric with the forward tunnel, using the same encapsulation method and endpoints. IP in IP encapsulation is assumed unless stated otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: The device finds a foreign agent that offers this service and asks for it when it registers. It then either sends its packets plainly to that agent, which wraps them, or wraps them itself and hands them over ready-made.

sections.title: The New Message Bits
sections.content:
Three formats change. The Mobility Agent Advertisement Extension gains one bit, the T bit, set by an agent that offers reverse tunnelling service. A foreign agent that sets it must support the Direct Delivery Style and should support the Encapsulating Delivery Style. A mobile node that does not understand the bit simply ignores it.

The Registration Request gains the same T bit, using one of the reserved bits. It asks the home agent to accept a reverse tunnel from the care-of address; a mobile node using a foreign agent care-of address asks the foreign agent to reverse-tunnel its packets. An agent that does not support reverse tunnelling rejects a request with the T bit set. In Registration Requests sent by a mobile node, the Time to Live field in the IP header must be set to 255.

The Encapsulating Delivery Style Extension may be included by the mobile node to further specify the behaviour. Its type is 130 and its length is 0. It is expected to be used only by the foreign agent, which must consume it rather than relay it to the home agent. It must not be included if the T bit is not set, and if it is absent Direct Delivery is assumed.
sections.plainLanguage: Two bits and one small extension carry the whole request. One bit says an agent offers the service, another says the device wants it, and the extension says which of the two ways the device wants.

sections.title: The New Denial Codes
sections.content:
Foreign and home agent registration replies must say whether a reverse tunnel request failed. The foreign agent codes are 74, requested reverse tunnel unavailable, 75, reverse tunnel is mandatory and the T bit not set, 76, mobile node too distant, and 79, delivery style not supported, which the document notes had not yet been assigned by IANA at the time of writing. The home agent codes are 137, requested reverse tunnel unavailable, 138, reverse tunnel is mandatory and the T bit not set, and 139, requested encapsulation unavailable.

A mobile node may receive code 70 from a foreign agent and code 134 from a home agent for a poorly formed request, and must accept them, but agents that support reverse tunnelling must use codes 74 and 137 respectively. A foreign agent that does not implement the Encapsulating Delivery Style must answer with code 79.

Forward and reverse tunnels are symmetric, so both can use the tunnelling options negotiated at registration. A home agent must therefore deny a registration if an unsupported form of tunnelling is requested, with code 139; Mobile IP already defines the analogous code 72 for the foreign agent.
sections.plainLanguage: Each agent has its own set of numbers for saying no, so the device can tell which side refused and why. Two of them mean the service is wanted but not available.

sections.title: The Two Delivery Styles
sections.content:
In the Direct Delivery Style, the mobile node must designate the foreign agent as its default router, otherwise not all of its traffic is guaranteed to be encapsulated and the reverse tunnel is defeated. The foreign agent must detect packets sent by the mobile node and modify its forwarding function to encapsulate them before forwarding. The encapsulating header carries the care-of address from the Registration Request as its source, the home agent address from the most recent successful Registration Reply as its destination, and protocol number 4 for IP in IP unless another method was negotiated at registration. This style is simple to implement at the mobile node and uses small packets on the link, but it only supports reverse tunnelling of unicast packets and does not allow selective reverse tunnelling.

In the Encapsulating Delivery Style, the mobile node does the encapsulation itself and addresses the foreign agent in a new outermost header. The foreign agent does not modify its forwarding function: it verifies that the packet came from the mobile node, decapsulates it, re-encapsulates it and sends it to the home agent. If it receives an unencapsulated packet from a mobile node that asked for this style, it must not reverse tunnel that packet and must forward it by ordinary IP routing. Mobile nodes that want to send broadcast or multicast packets must use this style, and so must mobile nodes that want selective reverse tunnelling.
sections.plainLanguage: With Direct Delivery the device sends plain packets and the foreign agent wraps them. With Encapsulating Delivery the device wraps them itself, which is more work but is the only way to send broadcast or multicast, or to leave some packets alone.

sections.title: What Each Party Checks
sections.content:
The foreign agent checks that the T bit is set and whether it can accommodate the request. If it cannot support the requested form of encapsulation it must return code 72, and if it cannot support the requested delivery style it must return code 79. It may reject a request without the T bit with code 75. It must verify that the TTL field of the IP header is 255 and otherwise reject the registration with code 76, and it must limit the rate at which it sends these replies to one per second. As a last check, it verifies that it can support a reverse tunnel with the same configuration, and must return code 74 if not. Otherwise it relays the Registration Request to the home agent, updates its visitor list with the reverse tunnel and the expected delivery style, and processes incoming traffic in that style.

The home agent checks whether it can accommodate the request, returning code 139 if it cannot support the requested encapsulation and code 137 if it cannot support a symmetric reverse tunnel. It may reject a request without the T bit with code 138. It then updates its mobility bindings list to record the reverse tunnel and the expected encapsulation.

After a successful registration the home agent may receive encapsulated packets addressed to itself. Decapsulating such packets and injecting them into the network blindly would be a weakness, so the home agent must implement, and by default should enable, a check: it searches for a mobility binding whose care-of address is the source of the outer header and whose mobile node address is the source of the inner header. If no such binding exists, or the packet uses an encapsulation mechanism that was not negotiated at registration, it must silently discard the packet and should log the event as a security exception.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side checks what it can support and says no with a specific code if it cannot. The home agent also checks that a tunnelled packet really came from a device it has a record for, and drops it quietly if not.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Creating both forward and reverse tunnels involves an authentication procedure, which reduces the risk of attack, and the extensions are subject to the security considerations of the Mobile IP specification. Once the tunnel is set up, a malicious node could hijack it to inject packets into the network, and reverse tunnels may make this worse because packets reaching the tunnel exit point are forwarded beyond the local network. Unauthenticated exchanges with the foreign agent let a malicious node pose as a valid mobile node and redirect an existing reverse tunnel to another home agent, perhaps another malicious node. The best protection is the Mobile-Foreign and Foreign-Home authentication extensions.

Where the necessary security associations are not available, the document introduces a weaker mechanism. The mobile node must set the TTL value in the IP header of Registration Requests to 255, which prevents malicious nodes more than one hop away from posing as valid mobile nodes. The Mobile IP Working Group considered other mechanisms using unauthenticated state, and rejected them because they introduce denial-of-service risks in exchange for weak protection.

On ingress filtering, the document notes the conjecture that administrators will target reverse-tunnelled packets, and quotes the ingress filtering recommendation's reasoning that tracking the source of an attack is simplified when the source is more likely to be valid. For disparate address spaces, the foreign agent selects the reverse tunnel using link-layer information, so the link layer must securely authenticate traffic from the mobile node; unauthenticated link-layer technologies such as shared Ethernet are not recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel can be hijacked to inject traffic, so the exchanges that set it up should be authenticated. Where that is not possible, the device sets a time-to-live of 255 so that only a host on the same link can pretend to be it.

sections.title: IANA Codes and Changes from RFC 2344
sections.content:
The Encapsulating Delivery Style extension is a Mobile IP registration extension, and IANA assigned the value 130 for it when RFC 2344 was published. The reply codes are error codes as defined by Mobile IP: IANA assigned 74 to 76 for the foreign agent rejections and 137 to 139 for the home agent rejections at the same time, and later assigned 79 for delivery style not supported.

The appendix lists the changes from RFC 2344. Appendix A on disparate address spaces and private addresses was added, along with the matching security consideration. Encapsulating Delivery Support was made optional, demoted from a MUST to a should, which required the new error code 79. The document mentions the possibility of an admissible authentication extension that differs from the Mobile-Home one, and an IANA considerations section was added.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbers used by this document were handed out by IANA. Compared with the 1997 version, this one adds guidance for private address spaces, makes the encapsulating style optional rather than compulsory, and explains the code assignments.
